<message id="issue:66" author="@nateprewitt" role="member" date="2026-03-18">
RFC: Adding inline type annotations to Requests

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Before reporting new issues,** be sure to check [this comment](https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/7271#issuecomment-4424268705) to see if your problem is already being addressed.

## Motivation

Requests has notably been without inline type annotations since type hints entered the Python ecosystem. We've had aspirations of bringing Requests up to par with community standards for a few years but have been unable to properly express the typing contract. This change doesn't solve all of those gaps, but does make progress towards that goal.

The maintainers of typeshed have provided an incredibly useful alternative for Requests typing for quite a while. There are some limitations of type stubs that can't fully express the Requests API though. Cases like `iter_content` having different return typing based on input, or PreparedRequests needing to be state checked can't be easily expressed. Inline annotations let us own the type contract alongside the code and should help drive better development decisions in the future.

Hey Nate, thanks for publishing that pre-release!

The class-level attribute annotations on `Response` are causing issues for downstream projects that subclass it as a dataclass or similar. Other classes in `models.py` surely have the same problem. It does seem that [enabling forward references](https://www.attrs.org/en/stable/types.html#forward-references) is the culprit downstream, so I wonder if this something that should be addressed here.

For example, in `requests-cache`:

```python
@define(auto_attribs=False, repr=False, slots=False)
class BaseResponse(Response):
    """Wrapper class for responses returned by :py:class:`.CachedSession`. This mainly exists to
    provide type hints for extra cache-related attributes that are added to non-cached responses.
    """
```

source: https://github.com/requests-cache/requests-cache/blob/5ca431fefa89001e09fd22da642867248aea2a01/requests_cache/models/response.py#L28-L32

FWIW moving the annotations to the attribute assignments inside `__init__` seems to fix the problem.

<message id="comment:253" author="@nateprewitt" role="member" date="2026-05-08">
Thanks for the repro, @edgarrmondragon. This is an unfortunately messy side-effect I was not aware of. Presumably this would apply to most dataclass style libraries beyond `attrs`?

I don't have a strong reason why these were added at class-level other than consistency. Not all attributes can be moved to `__init__`. Some like `Response.connection` or `RequestsCookieJar._policy` aren't actually set in the `__init__` (or don't have an explicit `__init__`). I tried in this [commit](https://github.com/psf/requests/commit/35ba878a7266b02bd392db1d57f7d06dc2ec71be) but these two top-level attributes are stuck where they are.

> FWIW moving the annotations to the attribute assignments inside __init__ seems to fix the problem.

Given the above, I'm curious how you aren't hitting errors for `HTTPAdapter` with `connection`. Do you have an example of what you tried?
</message>

<message id="comment:252" author="@edgarrmondragon" date="2026-05-08">
> Given the above, I'm curious how you aren't hitting errors for `HTTPAdapter` with `connection`. Do you have an example of what you tried?

If I move `RequestsCookieJar` outside of the `TYPE_CHECKING` block, _then_ I do get a similar error for `HTTPAdapter`

> Some like `Response.connection` or `RequestsCookieJar._policy` aren't actually set in the `__init__` (or don't have an explicit `__init__`).

I gave it a try locally and it seems you can still annotate it within `__init__`:

```python
class Response:
    def __init__(self, ...) -> None:
       self.connection: HTTPAdapter
```

I created a PR with the small diff I tried out locally, which fixed my requests-cache example above:

- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/7417

<message id="comment:251" author="@nateprewitt" role="member" date="2026-05-08">
I phrased my comment poorly. Mechanically, I agree it works to move the attributes into `__init__`, but adding a type in `__init__` that doesn't exist yet seems like we're lying about types to work around this use case. I'd like to avoid that if we can.

Trying to line Requests' classes up with dataclasses strikes me as odd to begin with since there's a fundamental tension between the two. One is trying to provide definitions, the other is focused on providing function. I don't actually know what is the best way to bridge this. If anyone watching this with experience working around this, feel free to add your thoughts. I can ping a few people as well for their thoughts.

It's a bit difficult to reason about how broadly this pattern is used. If it's a few libraries that need to tweak `attrs` or add `TYPE_CHECKING` imports, I'd prefer to help make those changes downstream. If it's hundreds or thousands of projects, then we have a bigger issue.
</message>
